nodes.summary: Adds a validated node to research.json without hand-editing JSON; splices textually so the hand-curated file keeps its grouping and comments.
caveats: Prefer -Json (or -JsonPath) for any prose containing apostrophes or quotes. Passing a summary as a quoted PowerShell string is how this catalog ended up storing assembly's: a single-quoted here-string doubled the apostrophe and nothing downstream could tell corruption from intent.

nodes.summary: Add a topic to the thread item list. Appends, and does NOT change what is active unless -Active is passed -- recording work for later no longer costs you your place.
caveats: Refuses a duplicate topic rather than creating a second entry that selectors cannot tell apart -- use Update-ThreadItem.ps1 to amend an existing one.

nodes.summary: Mark a thread item done. Retains it: Show-ThreadItems.ps1 -All prints completed items, so the list records what was finished and not only what is outstanding.
caveats: Does not auto-activate anything. Pop-ThreadStack promoted the next parked item automatically, which quietly decided what you worked on next; choose with Set-ActiveThread.ps1 instead.

nodes.summary: Encode a file's content as Base64 for use with New-TextFile.ps1 -Base64.
Converts Mermaid diagram source to an inline HTML img tag via mermaid.ink; can process whole markdown files.
caveats: Sends diagram source to mermaid.ink, a third-party service, encoded in the URL. The content leaves your machine -- check it against the PROVENANCE.md boundary before diagramming anything sensitive.
Output depends on that service staying up and on the reader being online; the img tag is a remote reference, not an embedded image.

nodes.summary: Two-pass non-ASCII to ASCII cleanup; handles raw Windows-1252 bytes in 0x80-0x9F that .NET's UTF-8 decoder silently destroys.

Queries a .NET XML documentation file the way Get-Research queries research.json: ranked free-text search returning parsed members (kind, declaring type, readable signature, summary, per-parameter docs) instead of grep hits. Exists because researching a library from raw doc XML is expensive and bad at the job -- the file is one stream of hard-wrapped indented <member> elements, so a match costs dozens of context lines and the answer arrives split across them. Flattens doc markup (see cref, paramref, c) into prose, shortens fully-qualified argument lists, and follows <inheritdoc/> chains transitively (BarSeries -> Series -> ISeries is the ordinary shape, and one hop makes results depend on document order). Resolves the .xml from the NuGet cache by package id, newest version and newest TFM, so callers never hunt for the path. JSON by default with the standard envelope; -Text to read at a terminal; -Package alone gives cheap orientation (counts by kind, largest types).
caveats: A bare <inheritdoc/> with no cref is NOT resolved -- implicit inheritance needs the type hierarchy, which an XML doc file does not carry. Those members read as undocumented even though the base or interface documents them; check the base type by name when a result looks empty.

Only reads XML that ships inside the package under lib\<tfm>\. Packages built without GenerateDocumentationFile throw a clear error rather than returning nothing, and a package documenting only some members will honestly report the rest as undocumented.
Generic arity survives in names as it does in the file (Series`3, CoreAxis`2), so query by simple name rather than pasting a C# generic.

nodes.summary: Report a compiled assembly's real API -- types, their declared members, and their base types -- by reflection. REACH FOR script.get-api-doc FIRST: most packages ship an XML doc file and that answers the same question with prose summaries and per-parameter docs, cheaply. Use THIS when the XML is absent, when a member is undocumented (XML carries only what was documented), or when the inheritance chain itself is the question -- reflection reports what the compiler emitted rather than what someone wrote down. Handles the two things that make the naive attempt fail: it resolves DEPENDENCIES from the folder the assembly sits in (loading straight out of ~/.nuget/packages/<pkg>/lib/<tfm>/ throws ReflectionTypeLoadException because that folder holds one DLL alone -- measured: 251 loader errors), and on a partial load it uses the types that did load while reporting how many did not. Filters before printing, because GetTypes() on a compiler library returns hundreds of types. Declared members only by default, compiler-generated accessors (get_X/set_X) suppressed. Written 2026-08-11 while hand-reflecting Loretta's Lua syntax types -- a job Get-ApiDoc could have done, and the reason the first line of this summary exists. The run did earn its keep: it showed obj:m() is a DIFFERENT node type (MethodCallExpressionSyntax) from f() (FunctionCallExpressionSyntax), which a guess would have missed silently and a switch statement would have dropped on the floor.
caveats: Point -SearchRoot at a build or publish output, not a nuget lib folder: dependencies must be side by side. The script prefers the candidate with the most sibling DLLs and warns when a load fails in a folder holding only one.

LoadFrom pins assemblies for the life of the PROCESS, and an agent shell reuses one process across commands. A sibling-resolution failure therefore reproduces only in a fresh process (pwsh -NoProfile -Command); once a dependency is loaded from anywhere, a later load from a folder missing it silently succeeds.
Public types only, and -MaxTypes caps the listing at 40 (truncated is reported, never silent).

nodes.summary: Inventories configuration files (JSON, YAML, XML) under a directory, with optional key sampling.

Queries the DriveSurvey inventory (D:\Repos\DriveSurvey): volumes ever seen including offline and silently-unmounted clone disks, sized subtrees, blind spots, volume-vs-volume coverage compare, and the indexed-vs-used reconciliation check.
caveats: Read-only against surveyed volumes and never deletes; scan refuses a docked drive that cannot prove which physical drive it is (the Sabrent bridge blanks hardware serials) -- answer with -Nickname.
compare matches by name + size until phase 2 adds content hashes; it finds missing coverage reliably but over-trusts renamed same-size files.

nodes.summary: LSP client that starts csharp-ls, indexes a solution, and finds all references for types and extension methods.
caveats: Requires csharp-ls on PATH (not currently installed). Install with: dotnet tool install --global csharp-ls
Indexing a large solution is slow and the script has no timeout, so a hung language server presents as a stalled session -- see pattern.circuit-breakers.

nodes.summary: Namespace inventory for a C# tree.
Scans a repo for .csproj files and produces a markdown summary of each project.
Queries research.json by id, tag, kind, or scored free text, returning a ranked top-N shortlist; the single retrieval entry point so startup never loads the full inventory.
caveats: -Text is denser than the JSON for multi-node results (75% of the size: it drops the per-node field names), so it is the cheaper form for a model scanning a shortlist -- the opposite of Invoke-JanetStartup, where -Text is 251% because it adds every rule why. Choose by what the projection contains, not the flag name. -Text is written with Write-Host, so it cannot be captured by pipe, > redirection, or assignment; use 6>&1. See note.startup-brief-budget.

nodes.summary: Lists all scripts with synopsis and parameter names by scanning the script directory; the exhaustive fallback when research.json lookup misses.
Reports types that share a short name across two C# codebases.
Maps Using Include directives across csproj files.

Resolves git.exe and forwards all arguments to it. git is not on PATH in every shell this repo is used from -- an agent session does not load the user profile that adds it -- and Visual Studio bundles a copy, so this finds it once rather than each caller rediscovering the path. Run with no arguments to get the resolved path on the SUCCESS stream, so "$g = & .\git.ps1" actually captures it; the RetirementCore counterpart uses Write-Host, which goes to the information stream and silently yields nothing. Git's own "-C <path>" forwards correctly (verified), which is how to operate on another repo without changing directory. Targets 5.1 as well as 7, since a shim that resolves a tool is exactly what gets run from whatever shell is open.
caveats: The candidate list leads with this machine's VS 18 Enterprise path. On another machine that misses and the fallback is a recursive Get-ChildItem over the Visual Studio install root, which is slow but only reached once per invocation.

nodes.summary: Manifest-driven build-and-deploy orchestrator: the generic pipeline (validate-first, git identity stamp, build/package/push gates, stamp-after-push, health poll distinguishing warming from broken, promote hint) lives here; each project declares only nouns in a deploy-manifest.json. Deploy sibling of the manifest-startup pattern.
caveats: Manifest command lines execute as trusted code in the repo root - the manifest is project config, not untrusted input. Only push type azureWebAppZip exists so far; add types in the switch when a new target platform appears. Verify counts only HTTP 200 as healthy. Get-Prop uses the Properties indexer deliberately: .Properties.Name -contains throws under StrictMode when the JSON object is empty.

nodes.summary: Build + test a .NET target and report as structured JSON (contract 3) instead of console scrollback: { contract, target, configuration, succeeded, build: { succeeded, durationSeconds, errors[], warnings[], warningCount, newWarnings, resolvedWarningCount, baseline }, tests: null | {...}, graph: null | { path, builtAt, newestSourceAt, status, refreshed, canRefresh } }. errors[] verbatim; warnings[] grouped by code with an honest omittedInstances marker; -New diffs the census against the previous -New run (newWarnings uncapped/verbatim). failures[] carry the whole assert message and file:line, read from TRX not scraped. CODE GRAPH: in a repo carrying the convention (.graph dir + scripts\graph.ps1) a successful build refreshes the graph when source has outrun it (~12s on a mid-size solution), because the check loop is exactly what bypasses the repo build script and leaves an agent querying a stale graph; staleness is REPORTED even when it cannot be fixed. Exit code means exactly one thing: 0 iff build succeeded and every test passed. WHEN: any dotnet build/test a session runs; -New when the question is what did THIS change introduce; -NoGraph for the fast path.
caveats: Contract drift check: the envelope stamps contract (currently 3). If the number differs from this node, or fields appear that this summary does not list, the contract has moved -- trust the JSON in front of you, re-read the script help, and update this node rather than assuming this summary.

Warnings report what dotnet emitted THIS run. Without -New an incremental no-op build legitimately shows 0 warnings, and NU-prefixed restore warnings replay only when restore actually runs. -New neutralizes both by forcing --no-incremental AND --force -- slower, but the census is complete; plain runs stay fast and incomplete.

The -New diff keys on file|code|message: a warning that merely moved lines is not new, and the same message twice in one file merges to one key. WPF temp-project names (App_<random>_wpftmp.csproj) are canonicalized to the source project at parse time -- the random infix would otherwise churn the diff every run.

The baseline is a rebuildable cache under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Janet\dotnet-check, keyed by target+configuration; wrong-contract baselines are silently treated as absent and rewritten. Only a successful build saves one -- a failed build is a partial census.

Graph refresh is DELEGATED to the repository's own scripts\graph.ps1 and only runs when the build succeeded and source has outrun the graph; a failed build is never graphed. graph:null means the repo has no graph convention (not applicable), NOT that a graph is missing. Staleness is reported even where canRefresh is false.
dotnet test runs with --no-build against the just-built output; a -TestFilter changes the counters to describe the filtered run, not the whole suite.

nodes.summary: PreToolUse hook that denies direct Write/Edit of research.json and points at the validating add/update scripts.
caveats: Wired twice: project-level .claude\settings.json (live only when JanetHome is the project dir) and user-level ~\.claude\settings.json by absolute path (2026-08-01, skips when the project dir IS JanetHome so the levels never double-fire). Guards by leaf name, so a file named research.json in ANY repo is denied when the user-level hook is active.

nodes.summary: Circuit-breaker wrapper for external commands (DESIGN-NOTES section 8 as code): captured StdOut/StdErr as line arrays, explicit timeout with kill, throws on failure by default; -NoThrow/-Quiet for caller-owned outcomes, -WorkingDirectory defaults to the caller's PowerShell location.

Executes startup-manifest.json: sets $env:JanetBase, validates every entry resolves before running anything, executes startup commands, emits a trimmed session brief (-Full for everything, -Text for the terminal).
caveats: Trims by default (-Full restores): strips $-prefixed manifest keys, reduces retrieval to graph/via/hint, emits rule text without why, omits run output already in captured. enforcedBy verification recognizes TWO wirings: project-level (Join-Path <project dir> <enforcedBy>) and user-level (~\.claude\settings.json names the script AND it exists at repo root) -- so ENFORCED labels survive foreign-dir sessions on this machine. An unwired hook NEVER fails startup: the rule is relabelled ADVISORY (claims ENFORCED; hook not wired here) and the note goes to the brief's own enforcement field plus the warning stream, NOT to problems (Start-Janet gates launch on problems). Only unresolved manifest entries are fatal, governed by onMissing. Runs from any working directory: everything resolves from $PSScriptRoot. Writes .janet\last-brief.json every run INCLUDING -Text; -OutFile moves it, an empty -OutFile skips writing. Adding a parameter renames every same-named local: $full/$text collided with -Full/-Text. See note.startup-brief-budget.

nodes.summary: PostToolUse hook that lints any .ps1 immediately after it is written, returning violations as context.
caveats: Wired twice: project-level .claude\settings.json (live only when JanetHome is the project dir) and user-level ~\.claude\settings.json by absolute path (2026-08-01, skips when the project dir IS JanetHome). The user-level wiring lints every .ps1 written in ANY session on this machine against the JanetHome house rules -- deliberate, they are personal rules, but remember it when a lint message appears in an unrelated repo.

nodes.summary: Bulk namespace rename across csproj Using directives and .cs using statements.

PreToolUse hook enforcing RESEARCH FIRST: writing a NEW .ps1 into a scripts directory is denied unless Get-Research.ps1 has run recently. The denial is not a nag -- it runs the catalog query itself on terms taken from the file name and hands back the closest existing nodes, so the answer arrives with the block. Clearing it is one command, which is the command that should have been run. Written 2026-08-11 after Get-AssemblyApi.ps1 was authored while script.get-api-doc already answered the same question; nothing was violated, because the manifest explained HOW to query the catalog and never said TO. Deliberately narrow: creation only, .ps1 only, scripts/ only -- the moment a duplicate tool becomes permanent is when it is authored, and a guard that fires on everything gets clicked past. Get-Research.ps1 leaves the trace (-NoTrace suppresses it, used by the guard's own lookup so it cannot clear the check it is about to make). Graph-first is a technique for once you know what you are building; this ranks above it.
caveats: Wired in TWO places and needs both: .claude/settings.json arms it when the project dir is JanetHome, and ~/.claude/settings.json arms it by absolute path everywhere else. The failure that motivated it happened while the project dir was a DIFFERENT repo, so project-level wiring alone would not have caught it.

The trace is one file in the temp directory, so concurrent sessions share it -- one session's query clears another's guard. Accepted, not solved: the check is a prompt to think, not a security boundary.
Fires only on Write of a new .ps1 directly inside a folder named 'scripts'. Notes, source files, and edits to existing scripts pass untouched.

nodes.summary: Applies a batch of surgical code edits from a JSON plan file; supports dry run and skipping build/test.
Generates an HTML status page for local Git repositories.
caveats: lib\Invoke-External.ps1 dependency restored 2026-08-02 (see script.invoke-external); no longer broken on that account, but not yet re-tested end-to-end.
Still calls New-TextFile.ps1 at $HOME\.github\scripts\, a path from the previous repo layout, and defaults -RootPath to C:\repos.

nodes.summary: Create or overwrite a text file without PowerShell here-string, escaping, or BOM pain; Base64 input mode sidesteps quoting entirely.
Opens a file in a specific running Visual Studio instance via COM (ROT + EnvDTE).
caveats: Windows-only and requires an already-running Visual Studio instance; COM/EnvDTE has no equivalent elsewhere. This is the least portable script in the toolkit.

nodes.summary: Read cached JSON files as PSCustomObjects, with optional schema discovery.
Read a text file with automatic encoding detection.

Generic JSON-blob search with Get-Research conventions: orientation view (arrays + field census), scored -Query, prop=value -Where filters with wildcards and dotted paths, -Select projection, { returned, totalMatches, truncated, items } envelope, -Text opt-in. Built 2026-08-01 for querying saved RazorGraph graphs without the MCP server; works on any JSON file whose interesting content is an array of objects.
caveats: Loads the whole file into memory (fine for MB-scale graphs). Unlike Get-Research it caps -Where results too (default -First 10) because blob arrays can hold tens of thousands of items; -All lifts the cap and the envelope always says when it was applied.

nodes.summary: Set which thread item is active, by -Topic substring, -Index, or -None to clear. Focus is explicit rather than positional -- the stack made the top of the stack active by definition, so changing attention meant mutating the list.
caveats: An ambiguous -Topic is an error, never a first-match guess: the operation rewrites the file, and silently amending the wrong item is how notes get lost.

nodes.summary: Configure WER LocalDumps so a crash leaves a dump instead of only an event-log entry. Exists because a native access violation is not a managed exception: it bypasses DispatcherUnhandledException, UnobservedTaskException and AppDomain.UnhandledException alike, so a crash log written from those handlers stays empty -- an empty log is the signature of ANY native fault and says nothing about the cause. DumpType Mini gives stacks and modules (small, names the faulting module); Full adds process memory, which is what a use-after-free needs since the question is what the memory at the faulting address used to be. DumpFolder is written REG_EXPAND_SZ so %LOCALAPPDATA% expands per-user at fault time -- pass it unexpanded. Reads back after writing rather than trusting the write. -List needs no elevation; -Remove restores default behaviour. WER reads the key at fault time, so nothing restarts.
caveats: Setting or removing needs an elevated shell (LocalDumps is under HKLM); the script checks first and throws a clear message rather than surfacing an access-denied that reads like a missing key. -List works unelevated.
Full dumps are large -- a UI process with native rendering can produce hundreds of MB each, which is why DumpCount defaults to 3 rather than the usual 10. Remove the key once diagnosis is done.

nodes.summary: Show the thread item list as { count, active, items[], error }, each item being { topic, status, refs[], next, notes }; -All includes completed items.
caveats: Runs in the startup path so it never throws: an unreadable or corrupt list is reported in-band via the error field with an otherwise empty envelope, rather than taking the session down.

nodes.summary: Launcher: runs Invoke-JanetStartup.ps1, refuses to launch on any problems entry, then starts an interactive claude session with the brief as the opening prompt. -Path for the working dir (default cwd -- designed for loading Janet while working in another repo), -DryRun to preview, prompts over 24k chars staged through a temp file.
caveats: Gates launch on the brief's problems field, so anything added to problems becomes a launch blocker by contract -- enforcement notes went there briefly on 2026-08-01 and broke launching from any non-JanetHome directory, the launcher's primary case. Unwired-hook notes now arrive in the separate enforcement field, printed as yellow warnings without blocking. Windows caps a command line at 32767 chars with silent truncation, hence the 24k inline-prompt ceiling.

The prompt is ALWAYS staged through a file; only a quote-free pointer goes on the command line. Passing the brief inline shredded under Windows PowerShell 5.1 native-argument passing (embedded JSON quotes are not escaped), and claude read brief fragments as options: error unknown option -Query, 2026-08-01.

nodes.summary: Deep-nesting (christmas-tree) detector for PowerShell by AST - the PS backend of the style gate nesting rule, sibling of RazorGraph deep_methods. Reports functions and top-level script bodies nesting >= MinDepth, deepest first; elseif adds no depth (free from IfStatementAst.Clauses); script-block literals count one level because they indent. JSON envelope, -Text opt-in, exit 1 on findings so it gates directly. Calibration 2026-08-03 over JanetHome scripts: >=3 flags 35 containers, >=6 flags 3; gate threshold set to 6 from that data plus the RazorGraphTool precedent (5 is case-by-case).
caveats: Parse errors are reported and exit 1, never silently skipped - an unparseable staged file fails the gate by design. Counting script-block literals is a deliberate divergence from the C# metric (lambdas add no depth there): pipeline-style trees would otherwise vanish from the report.

nodes.summary: Pre-push audit: scans files for non-ASCII bytes and line ending issues.
Lints .ps1 files against the mechanically checkable house rules: return @() unrolling, $null comparison order, truncating New-Item, plus 7-only syntax when -Target Ps51.

Repo-agnostic pre-commit gate: PSScriptAnalyzer, deep nesting (christmas-tree, fail at >=6), Pester, config check, encoding audit. Staged files resolve against git rev-parse --show-toplevel from the CWD, so the one gate serves every repo (the Janet-level decision in note.pre-checkin-style-janet-level). Resolves git via JANET_GIT, then PATH, then the VS-bundled copy - no machine-specific hardcoding.
caveats: Test-Config.ps1 remains absent; that step self-skips.

$LASTEXITCODE is reset before each child-script step: a child that never calls exit leaves the previous child code in place, and the encoding step once failed on the nesting step verdict while printing All clean (caught by the 2026-08-03 smoke test).
C# nesting is not checked per-commit - no fast syntax-only path yet; the C# rule lives in RazorGraph deep_methods / query --deep at repo level.

Module requirements are conditional and fail legibly when unmet: PSScriptAnalyzer only when .ps1 files are staged, Pester 5+ only when *.Tests.ps1 files exist. Both installed CurrentUser 2026-08-03 (PSScriptAnalyzer 1.25.0, Pester 6.0.1); full gate verified green end-to-end on a clean staged file the same day.

nodes.summary: Dot-sourced read/write/lock helpers for the thread item list: Read-ThreadItems (normalises every entry to topic/status/refs/next/notes), Write-ThreadItems, Invoke-ThreadItemsUpdate (mutex-guarded read-modify-write) and Find-ThreadItemIndex (resolves a selector to exactly one item, refusing ambiguity).
caveats: Not a standalone script -- it defines functions and does nothing when run.
Deliberately does NOT Set-StrictMode: strict mode in a dot-sourced file leaks into the caller scope. Each entry-point script sets its own.

Read-ThreadItems comma-wraps its return. Assign it; never wrap the call in @(...) -- that yields one element holding the real array and the loop runs once (house rule 1). This trap bit during the 2026-08-08 migration and was caught only by running the script.

nodes.summary: Publishes an MCP server to a fresh build-<stamp> directory and repoints a "current" junction at it, so a rebuild never contends with the running server. Client config names the junction and never changes again -- a stable path that resolves to the newest build by lookup. HTTP servers are stopped and restarted from the junction (measured: 1.9s from rotation start to serving again, against a ~31s reconnect backoff window, with the publish happening while the old server was still serving). stdio servers are left alone because the client owns the process: the win there is that the publish SUCCEEDS with sessions attached, and each new session picks up the newest build. Smoke-tests the new binary before repointing, keeps the last N builds for rollback, and skips pruning anything still locked.
caveats: Redirects BaseOutputPath only, never BaseIntermediateOutputPath. Moving obj\ stops MSBuild excluding the project's ORIGINAL obj\ from the default source glob, so both copies of the generated AssemblyInfo.cs compile and every assembly attribute collides with CS0579. The lock is on bin\; moving obj\ solves nothing and breaks the build.

MULTI-SESSION: -ProcessName stops only servers running from under -Root whose command line carries --http. Stopping by process NAME would also kill stdio servers belonging to other sessions, and stdio is never reconnected automatically -- those clients lose their tools silently, with no error and no recovery short of restarting. A rebuild must not be able to do that.

PRUNING CHECKS BEFORE DELETING, never delete-then-catch. Remove-Item -Recurse deletes what it can and only then throws, so a build with a live server loses every file the process has not currently mapped: measured 4 of 11, including the .deps.json the runtime needs for an assembly it has not loaded yet. The server survives until it reaches for one. Catching afterwards and reporting "kept" describes a directory already gutted.

A second session starting mid-rotation gets the newest build through the junction while an existing session keeps the one it started with, so two sessions can run different builds. That is inherent to stdio and harmless per-session, but it is the same version-skew note.razorgraph-cli warns about between the CLI and the MCP server -- check which build answered before trusting a disagreement.
Junctions are a Windows filesystem feature. A cross-platform port needs a symlink or a launcher shim that resolves the newest build.

-ToolProject packs and reinstalls global tools in the same pass. The CLI is NOT rotated -- a global tool is a separate copy on PATH -- so rebuilding the server leaves it stale, and a stale CLI reports a new verb as unknown while the server serves it fine. That was written down in a caveat and still caught us three times; the parameter is the structural fix a note could not be. Uninstalls then installs, because dotnet tool update no-ops on an identical version.

nodes.summary: Updates an existing research.json node in place with validation; preserves unknown fields and splices textually so the file keeps its curation.
caveats: Prefer -Json (or -JsonPath) for prose. The JSON form is a PATCH: only the fields present are touched, and it registers them as bound parameters so the same change-detection applies as the named-parameter form.

nodes.summary: Amend an existing thread item in place -- notes, resume cursor, refs, or status -- preserving every field not named; -AppendNotes and -AppendRefs accumulate rather than replace.
caveats: The operation the push/pop stack never had, and the reason it lost data: on 2026-08-08 a session wanting to update its own entry had only push and pop, popped to reach it, and destroyed a concurrent session notes irrecoverably. A missing operation does not leave callers stuck -- it makes them improvise with a destructive one.
